newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Brash says currency can't rise indefinitely.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Brash says currency can't rise indefinitely.

text.p: Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Don Brash said on Thursday that the current mix of monetary conditions was very unfortunate but the central bank could not determine it.
Brash, replying to questions after a speech in Christchurch, also said the exchange rate could not continue to rise indefinitely.

He said the fiscal stance of the new centre-right coalition government was less expansionary than some people had expected, but still meant the Reserve Bank had to maintain somewhat tighter monetary conditions than would otherwise be the case.
"The exchange rate is obviously an enormous source of worry to almost everybody in the export sector," Brash said.

"Without commenting on the level of monetary conditions, but simply about the mix of monetary conditions, the present mix with steadily declining interest and a steadily rising exchange rate is by no means optimal in terms of trying to control inflation in New Zealand today.

"There isn't much inflation coming out of the tradeable sector. More inflation is coming out of the non-tradeable sector which is really not much affected by the exchange rate, so the mix is very unfortunate."

Brash added: "Unfortunately, no central banks that I am aware of have worked out how they can control the mix of conditions. You can tighten policy, you can ease policy, but you can't determine that the easing takes the form of easing interest rates or exchanges rates or some combination of both."

Brash said the best evidence of that was the New Zealand experience of the last two or three months. Since September there had been a "huge reduction" in interest rates but the exchange rate had risen strongly over that period, Brash said. He cited New Zealand's high reputation in fiscal and monetary policy as one of the reasons for this.
Brash said people were willing to invest in New Zealand dollar assets even though interest rates were steadily declining.

"I guess logically... the process... can't go on indefinitely," he said. "At some point, people will start saying 'the export sector is shrinking, the balance of payments deficit is getting larger', and at that point the perception of risk in holding New Zealand dollars rises and we get some rebalancing of higher interest rates and lower exchange rate.
"But certainly there hasn't been much sign of that in the last wee while." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
